introduction-the-10000-surprise.core: Learners get huge bills by leaving resources running, misreading the free tier or leaking keys. The cloud won't stop spending on its own, so you need alerts, anomaly detection and hard guardrails.

first_principles.problem: A student follows a tutorial, forgets the database, and gets a $10,000 bill weeks later.
truths: Budgets alert; they don't stop anything by default.
derivation: Use **SCPs and account isolation** for teams.

analogy.title: Leaving the tap running in a rented flat
analogy.story: Nobody turns it off for you, and the water bill arrives at month end.
analogy.breaks: Providers sometimes forgive first-time mistakes, but don't count on it.

example.title: A safe setup on day one

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Surprises are caught within a day.

example.outcome: you can learn the cloud without financial risk.

check.q: Does setting an AWS Budget stop your resources at the limit?
check.a: No. By default it only sends alerts.

understanding-the-free-tier.core: The free tier is a set of specific allowances: 12-month offers (750 hours of t2/t3.micro), always-free quotas (Lambda requests) and short trials. Anything beyond the exact limits bills at normal rates.

first_principles.problem: People think 'free tier' means 'free account', then launch larger instances, extra volumes or NAT gateways that aren't covered.
truths: Allowances are per service and per type.
Hours are shared across all instances.
Many services have no free tier.
derivation: Check the **type of offer**: 12-month, always free, trial.
Remember that **hours aggregate**: two micro instances use 1,500 of 750 hours.
Watch the **non-free extras** (NAT, Elastic IPs, data transfer).

analogy.title: A buffet voucher for specific dishes
analogy.story: The voucher covers one salad and one soup; ordering the steak costs full price.
analogy.breaks: Offers change over time, so always check the current terms.

example.title: Two micro instances all month

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Free hours are a monthly pool, not per instance.

example.outcome: free tier usage stays genuinely free.

check.q: Why can running two free-tier-eligible instances still incur charges?
check.a: The 750-hour monthly allowance is shared across all eligible instances.

the-first-line-of-defense-aws-budgets.core: AWS Budgets alerts when actual or forecasted spend crosses thresholds you set. It's the first safety net, but it alerts rather than stops, unless you configure budget actions.

first_principles.problem: People assume a budget caps spending, and it keeps billing after the alert.
truths: Alerts need someone to act on them.
derivation: Alert at **50%, 80% and 100%** of actual and **100% forecast**.
Optionally add **budget actions** (attach a deny policy).

analogy.title: A fuel warning light
analogy.story: It tells you you're low; it doesn't refuel the car or stop the engine.
analogy.breaks: Billing data lags by hours, so alerts aren't real time.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: An email arrives the moment spend heads past $8.

check.a: It warns you when you're on track to exceed the budget, before it actually happens.

the-second-line-of-defense-cost-anomaly-.core: Budgets catch absolute totals at set thresholds. Cost Anomaly Detection uses ML to spot unusual patterns (a sudden daily spike in one service) even well below the budget, so problems are caught sooner.

first_principles.problem: A leaked key starts crypto-mining; the spend is unusual but still under the monthly budget for days.
derivation: Enable **Cost Anomaly Detection** monitors (per service, per account).

analogy.title: A bank's fraud detection
analogy.story: It flags an unusual purchase abroad even though you're within your credit limit.
analogy.breaks: New accounts have little history, so the model needs time to learn.

example.title: A leaked key incident
flow: GPU instances launched in new region

check.q: What can anomaly detection catch that a budget may miss?
check.a: Unusual spikes that are still below the budget threshold, such as a leaked key starting expensive resources.

the-third-line-of-defense-service-contro.core: For teams, alerts aren't enough. Use AWS Organizations: separate accounts per person or project for isolation, plus SCPs that deny expensive services, large instance types or unused regions, so certain spend is simply impossible.

first_principles.problem: A team member launches p4d GPU instances in an unused region, and alerts arrive after thousands are spent.
derivation: Give **one account per learner or project** (sandboxes).
**Restrict instance types** to a small allow-list.

analogy.title: Child-proof locks on dangerous cupboards
analogy.story: Instead of warning after the fact, the cupboard simply won't open.
analogy.breaks: Overly strict SCPs block legitimate learning, so provide an exception path.

example.title: An SCP restricting instance types

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: GPU or large instances simply can't be launched.

example.outcome: expensive mistakes are prevented, not just reported.

check.q: Why are SCPs stronger than budgets for preventing overspend?
check.a: They block the action entirely, even for administrators, instead of alerting after money is spent.
